mappings.note: Why producers always sit at the first trophic level - the structure of a food chain, C 2.8-LO-1, not the energy arithmetic of LO-2.

Conserving an endangered apex species. The frame has no biodiversity or conservation outcome - LO-2 is ozone, LO-3 is waste - so this rests at competency C 4.3 (interactions at ecosystem level) rather than being forced onto a food-chain outcome.
Why plastics resist micro-organisms - the mechanism behind LO-1's biodegradable/non-biodegradable distinction.
Steps taken to limit ozone damage - LO-2's 'measures taken to limit it' clause specifically, as against its causes clause.
Ozone as the shield and why UV harms organisms - the function and effects halves of C 4.3-LO-2.
Raw materials the first trophic level uses to make food (carbon dioxide, water) - producers as the base of the chain, C 2.8-LO-1.
Sorts six materials by biodegradability - LO-1's classification clause.

Which level transfers most and which receives least energy is decided by the ninety per cent loss at every step - the ten per cent law, C 2.8-LO-2. LO-1 would cover only the direction of flow, not the quantities being compared.
Picks the autotrophs (blue-green algae, grass) from a mixed list - assigning the first trophic level, C 2.8-LO-1.
Statement of the ten per cent law - C 2.8-LO-2's own subject.
Why man-made materials persist - the defining property of non-biodegradable substances, LO-1.
The five organisms must be ordered into a chain (C 2.8-LO-1) before biomagnification (C 4.1-LO-1) names the peacock; the item also asks for the phenomenon by name.
Naming household non-biodegradable wastes - LO-1's classification clause. It asks what they are, not how to dispose of them, so LO-3 is the wrong sibling.
Preventing accumulation of harmful chemicals in the body means limiting intake of non-biodegradable residues - the consequences clause of C 4.1-LO-1, the outcome that owns biomagnification.
Naming trophic levels on a diagram - C 2.8-LO-1. DEFECT: the figure the labels Z and X refer to is not stored, so the item cannot be answered from the text although its topic is unambiguous.
Halons in fire extinguishers destroy stratospheric ozone - the causes clause of C 4.3-LO-2.
Picks glass as non-biodegradable from bones, wool and paper - LO-1's classification clause.
Definition of an ecosystem. No outcome in this frame defines one, so it sits at competency C 4.3, which covers levels of biological organisation up to ecosystems.
Selecting biotic components from a list mixing living and non-living - ecosystem structure, which reaches no LO here, so competency level.
Jute and cloth are pushed because polythene is non-biodegradable; the reasoning asked for is the LO-1 distinction and its consequence, not an evaluation of disposal methods.
Segregation needs both outcomes: the two categories come from LO-1, and the reason for separating them - composting versus recycling or landfill - is LO-3's evaluation of disposal methods.
10,000 J at the first level gives 1,000 J at the second - a direct application of the ten per cent law, C 2.8-LO-2.
Herbivores always occupy the second trophic level - trophic structure, C 2.8-LO-1.
Requires ordering grass to hawk (C 2.8-LO-1) and then applying accumulation of a non-biodegradable pesticide (C 4.1-LO-1).
Constructing a food chain that includes humans - C 2.8-LO-1's 'constructs food chains' clause.
Producers versus herbivores in feeding habit - what defines the first two trophic levels, C 2.8-LO-1.
Naming natural ecosystems - ecosystem types, no LO in this frame, so competency C 4.3. Stored concept tag 'Energy Flow in Ecosystems' is wrong.
Biotic components of the biosphere - levels of biological organisation, competency C 4.3; no outcome covers it.
Why a forest or lake counts as a natural ecosystem - self-sustaining ecosystem structure, competency C 4.3.

Back-calculation from the lion to the producer applies the ten per cent law repeatedly - C 2.8-LO-2. DEFECT: the food chain is a figure that was not stored, so the number of steps cannot be read from the text.
500 J at the rats gives 50 J at the snakes and 5 J at the hawks - two applications of the ten per cent law, C 2.8-LO-2. Stem has mojibake arrows.
20,000 J at the plants leaves 200 J for man over two transfers - the ten per cent law, C 2.8-LO-2.
Abiotic components of an ecosystem - ecosystem structure, no LO in this frame, so competency C 4.3.
Building a four-level aquatic chain - C 2.8-LO-1's 'constructs food chains' clause, with no energy quantity asked for.
Biomagnification explained with an example; it happens because the toxin is non-biodegradable, which is C 4.1-LO-1's consequences clause. No chain is supplied to order.
Despite the preamble about higher trophic levels, the question asked is the BASIS of the biodegradable/non-biodegradable split plus examples - purely C 4.1-LO-1.
What ozone is and how it protects organisms - the function half of C 4.3-LO-2.

Part (a) names herbivores as primary consumers, a trophic-structure point (C 2.8-LO-1); part (b) computes the lion's 10 J from the plant's 1000 J, the ten per cent law (C 2.8-LO-2). The two parts test different outcomes.

Names biomagnification and justifies why humans carry the most - the retention of non-biodegradable chemicals, C 4.1-LO-1. No explicit chain is given to order, so the food-chain outcome is not indispensable.
Consequences of removing the lions or the deer from Grass-Deer-Lion - reasoning about the structure of a food chain, C 2.8-LO-1.

Anaerobic degradation is biodegradation without oxygen, which is C 4.1-LO-1. DEFECT: the other half, 'biomass', belongs to Sources of Energy and reaches no outcome in this chapter's frame; only the degradation half is mapped.
Why improper disposal of domestic waste is harmful and how to persuade people - LO-3's evaluation of disposal methods and proposals for reducing waste.
Formation of stratospheric ozone and its protective role - C 4.3-LO-2.

The ban is justified by polythene being non-biodegradable (LO-1) and the item then asks for alternatives and how the ban improves the environment, which is waste reduction (C 4.3-LO-3). Both are needed.

Why decomposers are essential - they break down biodegradable matter and return nutrients. C 4.1-LO-1 is the only outcome owning biodegradation; C 2.8-LO-1 concerns energy, which decomposers do not recycle.
Benefits of recycling - LO-3's waste-reduction clause. DEFECT: 'this recycling process' has no antecedent; the passage or figure it refers to was not stored.
Aerosol propellants are CFCs, hence the demand for a ban - the causes and measures clauses of C 4.3-LO-2.
Food web as branching food chains - C 2.8-LO-1 is the only outcome mentioning food webs.
Problems society faces from improper garbage disposal - LO-3's evaluation of disposal methods, framed as a values case study.
Arguments for recycling - the 'recycle' limb of LO-3's waste-reduction clause.
Individual environment-friendly practices - LO-3's 'proposes ways of reducing the waste a household generates'.
Why some substances are biodegradable and some are not - LO-1's distinction clause. DEFECT: duplicate of qid:87199, same stem from a different year's paper.
Justifying concern over ozone damage plus two limiting steps - the effects and measures clauses of C 4.3-LO-2.
Distinguishes the two classes and lists two environmental effects of each - both clauses of C 4.1-LO-1 and nothing beyond it, so no disposal code is added.
Formation, concern and cause of ozone damage - all of C 4.3-LO-2's causes and effects clauses.
The two halves map to different outcomes: effects of non-biodegradable substances (C 4.1-LO-1) and methods of safe disposal (C 4.3-LO-3). Neither half answers the other.

Ecosystem defined with its components, plus why an aquarium needs cleaning while a lake does not - natural versus artificial ecosystems. No LO in this frame reaches ecosystem structure, so competency C 4.3.
Pesticide residues in food grains arise because the chemicals are non-biodegradable and are retained as they pass along - C 4.1-LO-1's consequences clause. No specific chain is given to order.
Two distinct demands: justify unidirectional energy flow (C 2.8-LO-1) and explain how non-biodegradable pesticides enter and accumulate in the body (C 4.1-LO-1).
Differentiating the two classes is C 4.1-LO-1; the two habit changes for disposing of non-biodegradable waste are C 4.3-LO-3. Both halves are asked explicitly.
